quote: Inasmuch as God ordered Joshua to plant an ambush in their rear, that is, to plant warriors in hiding to ambush the enemy, we can learn that such treachery is not unjustly carried out by those who wage a just war. Thus, a just man, if he wishes to undertake a just war, ought to think chiefly in these matters about nothing else than whether it is right for him to do so, for it is not lawful for everyone to wage war. However, once he has undertaken a just war, it makes no difference to the justice of the war whether he wins in open warfare or by treachery. However, those just wars ought to be defined as those which avenge injuries, if the tribe or state which is about to be sought in war, either neglected to punish a crime improperly committed by its own countrymen or neglected to repay what had been lost through those injuries. Moreover, without doubt that type of war is just which God…

When these things have been heard, it is likely that the hearers will say: what is this to me? What does it profit me if I come to know that those who inhabited Ai were conquered, as though similar or even more powerful wars had not been waged or are not being waged? Was this the care of the Holy Spirit, that, leaving aside the destructions of so many and so great and noble cities, the battle of the city of Ai should be written and consigned to the sacred volumes? Perhaps what we are doing is rash, in that we attempt to explain places of Holy Scripture so lofty and so difficult; but if you aid us with your prayers, we shall not only escape the fault of audacity, but also God the Father of the Word, embracing our devotion, "will give a word for the opening of our mouth," whereby both you may be edified and we may appear not undevout. Praying, therefore, and attentive in mind, listen.…

We entreat you, O hearers of the sacred volumes, not to listen with weariness or distaste to the things that are read, on the ground that their narrative seems to be less delightful. For you ought to know that the things which are read are indeed worthy of the utterance of the Holy Spirit, but for explaining them we have need of that grace of the Holy Spirit of which the Apostle speaks: "to one, moreover, is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit." We too, then, have need of these things in the present passages, in which it is related that Jesus succeeded Moses, and that he himself leads the people, and a certain such history is prefigured in the present reading. Those who inhabited the city of Ai at first seemed indeed to conquer and to turn back the sons of Israel because of the sin which they had committed. But…

But perhaps you may say to me: how, then, is the former people set as though fleeing? And quite consistently. For those who follow Jesus were seen to flee from the legal burdens and precepts, from the observance of the sabbath, from the circumcision of the flesh, from the slaughter of victims. But again he who has followed Christ, the perfection and fullness of the law, does not flee.

But something else also occurs to me as I consider in this place "Jesus fleeing from the face" of the army of Ai. What do you think it is that "Jesus fleeing" signified? Let us see whether perhaps there is something which we conquer by fleeing, and there is some perfect virtue in flight. Paul the Apostle teaches us, saying: "flee fornication." You see, then, that there is a certain "spirit of fornication," which we ought to flee, whoever of us wishes to remain chastely and piously and modestly in Christ. This flight, then, is the one which has salvation; this flight is of virtue; this flight confers blessedness. And not only is the spirit of fornication to be fled, but in like manner, just as it was said, "flee fornication," let us hear it said to us: flee anger, flee avarice, flee envy and spite, flee detractions and evil-speakings. And yet I know not whether anyone escapes these, I…

But let us see what is also written in what follows: "and they struck them," he says, "with the edge of the sword, until there was not left of them one who might be saved, nor who might escape." When the Jews read these things, they become cruel and thirst for human blood, thinking that the saints too struck those who inhabited Ai, so that "there should not be left of them one who might be saved, nor who might escape," not understanding that in these words mysteries are foreshadowed, and that this is rather indicated to us, that of these whose dwelling is chaos and who reigned in the abyss, of the demons, we ought to leave none at all, but to slay them all. But we slay the demons not by destroying their very substance; but because their work and their zeal is this, to make men sin, and this is their life, if we sin, without doubt it is their destruction, if we do not sin. Therefore the…

But let us see what follows in the sequel: "and Jesus burned Ai," he says, "and it was made a wasteland, that it should not be inhabited forever." You see that these things which follow pertain more to the truth of the mystery than of the history. For that place of earth is not so much uninhabitable forever as the place of the demons will then be uninhabitable, when now no one will sin, "neither will sin reign" in anyone, when the devil and his angels will be delivered to eternal fire, our Lord Jesus Christ sitting as king and judge and saying to those who conquered, both the first and the last: "come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom which has been prepared for you by my Father." But to the others he will say: "go into the eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels," until he takes counsel with remedies for every soul, for those whom he himself knows,…

But after all things, even "the king of Ai" is said "to be hanged upon a double wood." In this place a mystery is concealed which lies hidden from very many, but, with you praying, we shall attempt to open these things not by our own opinions, but by the testimonies of divine Scripture. In the foregoing we said that the king of Ai may be compared to the devil; here it is worth the effort to know how "he is crucified upon a double wood." The cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was double. Perhaps what I say seems to you a strange and novel saying: that the cross was double, that is, it consists of a twofold and double reasoning; because visibly indeed the Son of God was crucified in the flesh, but invisibly upon that cross the devil with "his principalities and powers was affixed to the cross." Will this not seem true to you if I produce for you the Apostle Paul as witness of these things?…

But if perchance there is some more attentive hearer, he can say: the form of the things done seems indeed to be fitting, but this still troubles me, that the devil and his army, as far as is shown by the figure of the history, was destroyed; and how do we still see both the devil and the contrary powers to prevail so greatly against the servants of God, that even the Apostle Peter with great caution forewarns and says that it must be observed that "our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour"? Let us see, therefore, whether in this too we can find something worthy of the utterances of the Holy Spirit. One coming of Christ was accomplished in lowliness, but another is hoped for in glory; and this first coming in the flesh is, by a certain mystical manner of speech, in the holy scriptures called his "shadow," just as the prophet Jeremiah also…

After Jesus had overthrown Ai, that is, chaos, and had removed all its inhabitants, it was fitting that he should offer to God, the Most High over all, some gift worthy of so great and mighty a victory. Let us see, then, what this is that he does after the victory: "Jesus," it says, "built an altar to the Lord God of Israel on Mount Ebal, and he made it just as Moses the servant of the Lord commanded the children of Israel. Now it is written in the law of Moses that the altar should be made of whole stones, on which no iron has been laid." And after "Jesus made the altar," he placed "there whole burnt offerings to the Lord and offered a sacrifice of salvation," and after the sacrifice "Jesus wrote upon the stones the Deuteronomy, the law of Moses, and he wrote it in the presence of the children of Israel. And all the elders of Israel and the judges and their scribes went before, on this…

But observe what praise is ascribed to those very stones of the altar. "Just as," it says, "the lawgiver Moses said, that the altar should be built of whole stones, on which no iron has been laid." Who do you think are these "whole stones"? The conscience of each one knows who is whole, who is uncorrupted, unpolluted, unstained in flesh and in spirit, who is that one on whom "no iron has been laid," that is, who has not received "the flaming darts of the evil one" of concupiscence, but has "quenched" them with "the shield of faith" and driven them back; or who is that one who has never received the iron of strife, the iron of war, the iron of quarrels, but has always been peaceable, always quiet and gentle, formed by the humility of Christ. These, then, are the "living stones" from which Jesus our Lord "built an altar of whole stones, on which no iron has been laid," that he might offer…

But the adornment of the altar is not yet complete, even if it be built "of whole stones," even if "iron" and "the dart of the evil one" be not found "laid" upon them, but there is still something lacking, and there is still what Jesus may add to all these. What is it? "Jesus wrote," it says, "upon the stones of the altar the Deuteronomy, the law of Moses, and he wrote it in the sight of the children of Israel." As for the "writing" — however the son of Nave was then able to inscribe "the law upon the stones of the altar," and, as far as he was able, to sketch out the types: let us for our part see how our Jesus "wrote the Deuteronomy on the living and whole stones." Deuteronomy is so called as it were a second legislation. If, then, you wish to see how, the first law having been weakened, Jesus writes a second law, hear him saying in the Gospels: "It was said to the men of old: You…

I am indeed moved by what Scripture added in what follows. "And Jesus wrote," it says, "upon the stones the Deuteronomy in the presence of the children of Israel." How he could have "inscribed" so great a book while the "children of Israel" were standing by and remaining there, so that they did not depart until the writing of so many lines was finished, or even how the stones of the altar could have borne the contents of so great a book — let these Jewish defenders of the letter, who are ignorant of the spirit of the law, tell me. How is the truth of the history demonstrated in this? But among them "to this very day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over their heart." But for us, "having turned to the Lord" Jesus, "the veil is taken away," because "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" of understanding. Our Lord Jesus, then, does not need much time to write the…

"But both the proselyte," it says, "and the native-born together, and half were beside Mount Gerizim and half beside Mount Ebal." How shall we explain these things also? Truly there is need of the help of God, that we may be able with our words to expound and set forth the divine words: who are the "half" who walked "beside Gerizim," and who are the "half" who, although they too are saved, could nevertheless not walk "beside Mount Gerizim," but walk "beside Mount Ebal." "Mount Gerizim" holds the blessings, but "Mount Ebal" the curses which threaten sinners. For "they appointed," as it is written in Deuteronomy, six tribes "for blessing on Mount Gerizim" — and these the tribes which are more noble and choice, that is, "Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin" — but the other six, more ignoble ones, "for cursing," among which was also "Reuben," who "went up to his father's bed…

These things indeed the histories of the ancients relate as deeds done; but how shall we refer this narration of the history to a mystical understanding, so as to show who these are who walk "beside Mount Gerizim" and who these are who walk "beside Mount Ebal"? I see it thus, that there are two kinds of those who through faith hasten and press on toward salvation: one kind of those who, kindled by desire for the heavenly promises, strive with the utmost zeal and diligence, lest even the least beatitude should pass them by, having a longing not only to receive the blessing and "to be made a part of the lot of the saints," but also to stand in the sight of God and to be always with the Lord. But there are others who also themselves press toward salvation, but are not so much inflamed with love of the blessings or with desires for the promises as they rather hold this before their view,…

"After these things" it is related that "Jesus read all the words of the law, the blessings and the curses, according to all that is written in the book of the law; nor was there any word out of all that Moses commanded which Jesus did not read in the presence of the whole assembly of the children of Israel." Easy indeed is the explanation of the history, how the son of Nave "read all the words of the law which Moses wrote, in the presence of the whole assembly of the children of Israel"; but how our Lord Jesus does this for his people, it does not seem to me idle to show. And I for my part judge that, "whenever Moses is read" to us and, through the grace of the Lord, "the veil of the letter is removed" and we begin to understand that "the law is spiritual," and that, for example, the law when it says "you shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain" said this not…

Attend, therefore, more diligently to the words of Scripture, which says: "There was not any word out of all that Moses commanded which Jesus did not read in the ears of the whole assembly of the children of Israel." And it adds also: "to the women and the children and the proselytes." Our Lord Jesus knows that there are other ears besides these fleshly ones, which he requires for the hearing of his words and for the hearing of the law. Hence also in the Gospel, after he had instructed them about the individual things that were needful, he adds and says: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear!" And surely, if he had said this of fleshly ears, it would seem superfluous; for no one who did not have ears had assembled to hear his words. But since he knew that the things which were said ought to be received in the ears of the inner man, that is, in the understanding of the heart — for what…
